meta.title: Who really said "The customer is always right"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Popularly pinned on Harry Gordon Selfridge, but the earliest 1905 record credits Marshall Field. Origin is genuinely uncertain — Selfridge only popularized it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The customer is always right'?
meta.ogDescription: Not coined by Selfridge. The earliest 1905 record credits Marshall Field; Quote Investigator calls the true origin uncertain. Selfridge popularized it in London.

answer.label: Not coined by Selfridge — earliest record credits Marshall Field
answer.sourceLine: The slogan is popularly pinned on Harry Gordon Selfridge, but its earliest documented appearance — September 1905 newspaper articles in Boston — credits the Chicago retailer Marshall Field, in whose store Selfridge worked his way up from stock boy to partner. Quote Investigator ↗ tentatively ascribes the adage to Field while stressing it is not certain he coined it; Selfridge is one of several retailers who later spread the phrase, not its proven author.

source.heading: Where the phrase actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Coined by Harry Gordon Selfridge — unsupported
“A client is always right,” an “old saying,” 1884

source.excerpt: “Broadly speaking, Mr. Field adheres to the theory that ‘the customer is always right.’”
trail: The earliest close match is a September 1905 article about Chicago’s Marshall Field, which said he adhered to the theory that “the customer is always right,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikipedia notes the phrase is variously credited to Marshall Field, his one-time employee Harry Gordon Selfridge, and John Wanamaker — with no proof of who coined it (Wikipedia ↗).
A legal precursor, “a client is always right,” appears as an “old saying” in an 1884 text, showing the pattern predates the retail slogan (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Verbatim from the September 1905 Boston Sunday Herald / Boston Daily Globe article on Marshall Field, as reproduced by Quote Investigator.

source.rightsNote: Short commercial slogans of this kind are not eligible for copyright, and this one has appeared in the printed record since 1905 — well before the 1931 U.S. cutoff — with no single identifiable copyrighted work as its source. It is free to quote.

author.name: Marshall Field
author.heading: About Marshall Field
author.metaLine: 1834–1906 · Chicago department-store magnate; mentor to Harry Gordon Selfridge
author.bio: Marshall Field built Chicago’s dominant department store and is the figure named in the earliest (1905) printed appearances of “the customer is always right.” He championed liberal returns and customer service at a time when caveat emptor ruled retail. Quote Investigator credits him with popularizing — and possibly crafting — the slogan, while cautioning that the true origin is uncertain and that he may have heard it from another retailer, or even from an angry customer, and decided to adopt it.

cite.sourceCitation: The Boston Sunday Herald, 3 September 1905, and The Boston Daily Globe, 24 September 1905, reporting on Marshall Field of Chicago; reproduced in Garson O’Toole, “The Customer Is Always Right,” Quote Investigator, 6 October 2015.

copyAttribution: Not coined by Harry Gordon Selfridge. The earliest documented use of "the customer is always right" (Boston newspapers, September 1905) credits Chicago retailer Marshall Field, and Quote Investigator calls the true origin uncertain. Selfridge — Field's former employee — helped popularize the slogan in London but is not its proven author.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: “The customer is always right” is a genuine early-1900s retail slogan, but pinning its authorship on Harry Gordon Selfridge overstates the evidence. The earliest record points elsewhere, and the true origin is honestly uncertain.

items.why: Selfridge is widely named as the source, but the phrase’s earliest documented use (September 1905) credits Marshall Field — in whose Chicago store Selfridge rose from stock boy to partner — and predates Selfridge’s own London store, which opened in 1909. He helped spread the motto, but no primary source shows he coined it (Quote Investigator ↗).

Field is named in the 1905 articles and is tentatively credited by Quote Investigator, but even QI cautions he may have adopted the line rather than invented it — and one Field biographer argued his actual maxim was the longer “Assume the customer is right until it is plain beyond all question that he is not” (Wikipedia ↗).
The Philadelphia retailer is another figure the slogan gets attached to, underscoring that it was a shared industry ethos, not one person’s coinage (Wikipedia ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: a shared early-1900s retail motto whose earliest known record — September 1905, Boston press — credits Marshall Field. Quote Investigator ↗ says Field popularized the slogan and may have crafted it, but calls the chronology uncertain; Selfridge, Wanamaker and César Ritz all became attached to it afterwards.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The phrase captured a genuine revolution in retail. In an era when caveat emptor — “let the buyer beware” — governed shopping and misrepresentation was common, department-store pioneers like Marshall Field, Selfridge and Wanamaker made liberal returns and customer satisfaction a competitive weapon. The slogan advertised that new posture.
Its very usefulness as a motto is why it spread so fast and attached itself to so many famous names — and why, a century later, it is hard to say who said it first.
detailsBody: A recurring claim is that the working policy was actually the more cautious “Assume the customer is right until it is plain beyond all question that he is not.” This hedged form — discussed on Wikipedia ↗ — suggests the snappy slogan is itself a compression of a more nuanced managerial rule.
context.pull: A shared industry ethos in search of an author.
